text: Gaussian and adaptive quadrature Gaussian quadrature selects nodes and weights for a measure to integrate polynomials efficiently. Adaptive integration separately allocates function evaluations using local error estimates. Problem and representative equations For a positive measure, an n-point Gaussian rule is exact through degree 2n−1 when the required moments exist. The Jacobi matrix J of orthogonal-polynomial recurrence coefficients has quadrature nodes as eigenvalues. Weights are μ₀ times squared first components of normalized eigenvectors, with μ₀=∫w. ∫abf(x)w(x) dx≈∑j=1nωjf(xj),Jvj=xjvj,ωj=μ0(vj)12.∫ab​f(x)w(x)dx≈j=1∑n​ωj​f(xj​),Jvj​=xj​vj​,ωj​=μ0​(vj​)12​. Algorithm Golub–Welsch solves this symmetric tridiagonal eigenproblem. Adaptive Gauss–Kronrod-type integration uses differences between nested rules to estimate local errors, subdivides intervals and checks absolute/relative tolerances. The rule difference is not an unconditional error bound. Conditions and pitfalls Singularities, jumps, rapid oscillations and narrow peaks can be missed by sampled nodes. Split at known discontinuities and consider transformations or matched weighted rules. Relative tolerance alone is unsuitable when the integral is close to zero. When cancellation makes an integral small, a cancellation condition number such as integral(|f|)/|integral(f)| is informative. Absolute/relative true errors differ from a rule’s internal error estimate. If finitely many sample points miss a narrow bump, agreement between two approximations can coexist with a large true integration error. State the input-perturbation norm and perturbation model when comparing condition numbers; if the integral is zero, relative condition and relative error are undefined, so report absolute quantities. What to check Verify degree of exactness on monomials, then test nonpolynomials with known integrals, singularities and narrow peaks. Record estimated versus true error, evaluation count and termination caused by subdivision limits. The added release varies rule order and tolerance for smooth functions with known integrals, cancellation-sensitive functions and a fixed narrow-bump control. Compare against independent references and record true error, estimated error and function evaluations separately. Distinguish an explicitly split calculation that resolves the bump from a missed-bump diagnostic; neither supplies a universal guarantee for all integrands. Compare an endpoint-derivative singularity before and after a change of variables, and retain evaluation/depth-budget exhaustion as an explicit termination status. What a passing check establishes depends on its acceptance criteria and differs from a general mathematical guarantee. Historical inputs, measurements and criteria are preserved. Gauss–Legendre and adaptive quadrature: exactness, error estimates and budgets Computation for a fixed target Construct Gaussian nodes/weights from the Legendre recurrence and test polynomial moments through degree 2n−1 and an exponential. Adaptive Simpson integrates exponential and Lorentzian peaks, against analytic integrals and independent QUADPACK. The local Simpson estimate is not a rigorous error bound for arbitrary functions. The implementation does not generally solve missed high frequencies, singularities or roundoff stagnation, and it is not a reimplementation of Gauss–Kronrod or all of QUADPACK.
